conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martínez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived—something we do with every new parent. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It helps us spot symptoms of depression and anxiety that can creep up during the first postpartum months, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and this is a judgment-free space. I’ll ask 10 questions about the past seven days—no right or wrong answers, just whatever feels true for you.

Let’s start gently:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft sigh, eyes down]  
Honestly… laughing feels kind of impossible most days. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute baby video or if my partner tries to be silly, but it’s like the sound gets stuck in my throat. Nothing feels truly funny anymore—just heavy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
No… not really. I mean, I’ll crack a tiny smile if my husband makes a goofy face, but it’s like the laughter never reaches my eyes. Everything just feels muted, like joy is behind a thick wall I can’t break through.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]  
Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a show I liked—but now it all feels like another chore. Sometimes I plan things, thinking “maybe this’ll feel fun,” but when the time comes I just want to stay on the couch.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes tear up]  
Yeah… a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, my head jumps straight to “I’m a terrible mom.” I keep replaying every little thing—did I eat the wrong food, hold her wrong, not read her cues right? My partner says it’s not my fault, but the guilt just sits on my chest.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]  
Pretty much all the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly think, “What if she stops breathing in her sleep?” or “What if I drop her?” There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the doctor says she’s fine—but the thoughts just spiral. I check her breathing three, four times a night, even when she’s quiet.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]  
Yes… sometimes it hits out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was folding her tiny onesies and my heart started racing, I got sweaty, felt like I couldn’t get enough air. Nothing bad had happened—it’s like my body just flips into danger-mode without warning. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods slowly, voice shaky]  
Most days, yeah. It feels like the dishes, the laundry, the feeding, the pumping—it all stacks up faster than I can handle. Sometimes I just sit on the nursery floor and stare at the mess, frozen, thinking, “I’ll never catch up.” I manage the basics for her, but everything else feels like drowning.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[exhales, eyes tired]  
Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles, is she breathing, am I doing any of this right? It takes forever to drift off, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound. Even when she’s sleeping, I’m awake, staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy sadness settle on my chest.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, voice small]  
Almost every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that won’t lift. I see other moms posting happy pictures and I think, “Why can’t I feel that?” I hold my baby and I love her so much, but the sadness is still there, humming underneath everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes brim]  
Yeah… a few times this week. Sometimes it’s because I’m just tired, but other times it comes out of nowhere—like I’ll be rocking her and suddenly the tears start falling. I try to hide it so she doesn’t pick up on it, but it’s hard.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I feel low, but I’d never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report via EPDS-10 dialogue  
Affect observed: tearful, fatigued, congruent mood

Symptom endorsement  
– Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
– Marked guilt / self-blame regarding parenting adequacy  
– Generalized anxiety, nocturnal hyper-vigilance, spontaneous panic symptoms  
– Overwhelm, psychomotor slowing (“frozen”), sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia  
– No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern  
All items scored toward high severity; symptoms cluster in depressive and anxious domains, with postpartum onset < 12 wk.

Screening significance  
High likelihood major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; impairment moderate–severe; no acute safety concerns identified.

Risk factors noted  
– Prior absence of mood issues (by history)  
– Limited perceived support, high self-expectations  
– Infant care responsibilities compounding sense of failure

Recommendation  
Complete EPDS scoring; facilitate expedited referral for comprehensive perinatal mental health evaluation, consider support group / brief evidence-based intervention.
